content.title: Official Blind Review #3
content.review:
This paper deals with the problem of translating natural language questions to SQL queries by incorporating relational structures in database schema and the question to query. 

Specifically, the authors proposed that existing methods of translating natural language to SQL queries cannot generalize well to unseen schemas. They then proposed their methods based on self-attention modules and graph representation of schemas. In addition, they exploited the heterogeneity of the schema-induced graph and designed various relations and corresponding relation-aware embeddings. Finally, the authors introduced a schema linking task that helps identify references in questions and the columns/tables in DB. 

Strengths: 
S1: The paper investigates an important and interesting problem of translating natural language to SQL sentences, which can potentially be significant in the applications of DB. 
S2: The paper clearly identifies the challenges and shortcomings of existing works, which is easy to follow. The analysis of related work is sufficient. 
S3: The idea of inferring soft relations between questions and words is novel and interesting.
S4: In the experiment part the authors made a visualization of how the alignment between question words and elements in the DB schema looks like, which clearly illustrates the effectiveness of schema linking, one main contribution of the paper. 

Weaknesses: 
W1: I think the main weakness of the paper lies within the organization and description of the Sec. 3 “RAT-SQL”. Specifically, the authors made many forward references that make it hard for readers to follow. 
e.g. 
a. On page 3, in Sec 3.1 “Problem Definition”, the authors referred the readers to Section 3.6, which I think is unnecessary as Section 3.6 introduces detailed solutions instead of introducing problem. 
b. On page 3, in Sec 3.2 the authors referred the readers to Table 1, which actually lies on Page 5. 

In addition, in Sec 3.7, the authors did not mention the objective function that is used for learning the decoder. Since the decoder outputs a syntax tree instead of ordinary sequences (e.g. in machine translation), I think it is necessary that the authors make clearer descriptions on how the objective function is chosen and how the decoder is learned. 

W2: The empirical evaluations of the method are somehow limited. For example, in “Related Work”, the authors mentioned that there are two publicly available datasets. So why didn’t the authors use both instead of one?

content.title: Response to Reviewer #3
content.comment:
Thank you for the great review and improvement suggestions! We agree with you and the other reviewers that text-to-SQL is an important application area that warrants further representation research.

We are already hard at work at improving the readability/clarity of the paper (particularly Sections 1 and 3) and will post an updated revision in the next few days, along with a summary comment here. You are right that the organization of Section 3 should be improved and some of the technical details need clarification. In the meantime, here are some short answers to your questions.

Q: What is the decoder objective?
As in Yin and Neubig (2007), the objective is to maximize the probability of the exact SQL AST $P$ on the output. At every timestep, the decoder chooses an action $a_t$ to expand the current AST by either applying a production rule or choosing a column/table for the schema. We fix the expansion order of each AST to be its depth-first traversal order. Thus, for each AST the decoder is trained to maximize the probability of its corresponding sequence of actions. The objective function is a total cross-entropy $\sum_t \log \Pr(a_t \mid a_{<t}, y)$ over all timesteps where each action probability is computed as described in Section 3.7.

We are happy to elaborate more if you like. The new revision will also contain more details that clarify the decoder architecture and training.

Q: Should we perform experiments on the WikiSQL dataset in addition to Spider?
While WikiSQL was the first large text-to-SQL dataset, the research community over the last year has primarily focused on Spider. This is because:
a)	WikiSQL only has one table, thus the problems of schema embedding (addressed in our work) do not arise.
b)	WikiSQL questions are generated by paraphrasing auto-generated templated questions, thus they are often artificial [1].
c)	WikiSQL supports a limited subset of the SQL grammar (for example, there are no SQL joins).

Because of these limitations, most of the issues our work addresses are not relevant to WikiSQL, and thus we focus on Spider. Besides, the research progress on WikiSQL has saturated around 90% [2].

[1]  Zhong, V., Xiong, C., & Socher, R. (2017). Seq2SQL: Generating structured queries from natural language using reinforcement learning. arXiv preprint arXiv:1709.00103.
[2]  https://github.com/salesforce/WikiSQL

content.title: Official Blind Review #2
content.review_assessment:_checking_correctness_: I assessed the sensibility of the derivations and theory.
content.review:
This paper proposes an algorithm to translate natural language questions into SQL queries. First, a question, columns, tables are encoded using bi-LSTMs. Then, relation-aware self-attention with a stack of layers is used. Scheme encoding and scheme linking is conducted to model the column/table references. Then, decoder by LSTM is used to output a sequence of actions. Experiments are executed using Spider dataset. The proposed algorithm is compared to several existing algorithms including ones with BERT, and shown to outperform ones without BERT.
My simple question is why the authors do not use BERT? If it brings much gain on performance, just try RAT-SQL+BERT, which will clarify the contribution of the paper more apparently. Otherwise, there should be some merit without BERT. Second question is that by looking at Table 2(c), a large portion of performance gain is brought by scheme linking. However, scheme linking part described in Sec. 3.6 seems somewhat heuristic. If this is the important part, more elaborate analysis is needed (including possibility to apply this part to other existing methods.)
Overall, although I think this research is important, it can not be accepted as a strong ICLR paper yet.

content.title: Response to Reviewer #2
content.comment:
Thank you for the great review! We are going to post an updated revision in the next few days, along with a summary comment here.

Q: Schema linking feels heuristic. Is it applicable to other text-to-SQL methods?
The key technical contribution of this work is the first unified framework (RAT) for embedding hard relational structure and “soft” induced relations jointly when learning contextual representations with Transformers. While Transformers excel at learning “soft” relations in unstructured data, and graph neural networks (GNNs) excel at learning patterns over existing “hard” relational structures (graphs), the RAT framework combines the representational power of both. Both schema embedding and schema linking simply arise as instantiations of this framework.

Schema linking itself is applicable generally. In fact, an earlier version of schema linking was present in IRNet [2]. However, the relational framework is crucial to properly learning contextual token representations. Guo et al. incorporated schema linking in non-relational way as independent features on the question words and corresponding column names. As a result, it contributes 8.5% to their accuracy [1; Table 4] whereas the RAT-based schema linking contributes 12.5% to our accuracy [This work; Table 2c].

The actual implementation of schema linking is less important. Ours is based on string matching and is relatively simple, but the RAT framework’s support for arbitrary relational features makes hand-designing such relations really easy. Other future implementations of the schema linking relation (including learned ones) can be straightforwardly expressed in the same encoder framework. In effect, this framework provides an opportunity to incorporate arbitrary relational features to improve text-to-SQL performance, which all the reviewers highlight as an important application.

We will emphasize this distinction and our list of contributions more clearly in the new paper revision.

Q: What would be the contribution of BERT to (or in contrast to) RAT-SQL?
Our experiments with BERT-Base so far have not yielded substantial improvements when combined with RAT-SQL and finetuned (namely, just +0.1%). We lacked the hardware capacity to fine-tune BERT-Large (3x the size of BERT-Base) at the time of submission. We _may_ be able to conduct an experiment with BERT-Large during the discussion period. However, in our opinion BERT augmentation is orthogonal to the paper contributions and should not be a condition for acceptance.

While RAT-SQL+BERT would provide an interesting result, we believe an important question instead is “Does RAT supersede BERT, vice-versa, or are their contributions orthogonal?” This requires an experiment where BERT is fine-tuned to augment to the _baseline_ model (without RAT). We are conducting this experiment right now with BERT-Base, and will include it in the next revision.
Note: An earlier version of this experiment three months ago on a slightly different baseline showed the BERT improvement over baseline to be 6%, roughly half of the 12.5% improvement we get with the RAT framework.
Note, however, that even if all other models on the Spider leaderboard use BERT-Large (which is not specified), it typically adds about 8% to their accuracy [1]. In contrast, the RAT framework adds 12.5% to the accuracy of our baseline [Table 2c].

Finally, our new model improvements developed after the submission deadline put RAT-SQL on top of the current leaderboard, even above BERT-augmented models. The dev set improvement over the next-best unaugmented model is now around 8.5%.

[1] https://yale-lily.github.io/spider
[2]  Guo, J., Zhan, Z., Gao, Y., Xiao, Y., Lou, J. G., Liu, T., & Zhang, D. (2019). Towards Complex Text-to-SQL in Cross-Domain Database with Intermediate Representation. In ACL 2019.

content.title: Official Blind Review #1
content.review_assessment:_checking_correctness_: I carefully checked the derivations and theory.
content.review:
This paper studies the problem of translating natural language questions into SQL queries to answer questions from databases. 

Strengths of the paper:
1. The research problem is of great value in applications, as users may not have expertise on writing a good SQL queries. The proposed algorithm can help to parse the input arbitrary queries into SQL standard queries.
2. The experiments were conducted on publicly available datasets, i.e., the Spider dataset that has been investigated in the previous work.

Weaknesses of the paper:
1. Many details of the equations and techniques are not clear. For instance, what do the notations $c_{i,0}^{fwd}$, $c_{i,0}^{rev}$ stand for in section 3.3?; what is $d_z$ and how to set $H$ in section 3.4? what does $\alpha_{i,j}^{(h)}$ work for in section 3.4?
2. The motivations of some techniques used in the paper are not clear. For instance, why do the authors apply BiLSTM but not other recurrent neural networks to obtain representations of the nodes in the graphs?  Are there other techniques to obtain embeddings of nodes in a network? There are a number of network embedding techniques having been proposed, for instance:
(a) A. Grover et al., Node2vec: scalable feature learning for networks, KDD 2016.
(b) Z. Meng et al., Co-embedding attributed networks, WSDM 2019.
3. The contributions of the paper seem not significant. The paper sounds like a technical report on the combination of some existing encoding and decoding techniques to the task, although the task is interesting. In terms of technical contributions, the authors are encouraged to state them explicitly and more clear.
4. Is the code of the proposed model publicly available? 

In sum, the task of the research is very interesting. But at the current version, the paper needs to be revised to make all the notations and techniques be more clear, and the contributions of the paper seems marginal.

content.title: Response to Reviewer #1
content.comment:
Thank you for the great review and the improvement suggestions! We agree with you and the other reviewers that text-to-SQL is an important application area that warrants further representation research.

First and foremost, you are right that Sections 1-3 need re-organization and important readability/clarity improvements. We are currently hard at work updating the paper and will post the new revision within the next few days. We have incorporated your suggestions and many other restructurings to make the presentation clearer and explicitly motivated.

Q: What are the key contributions of the paper?
This work makes the following three contributions:
	•	We develop the first unified framework for embedding hard relational structure and “soft” induced relations jointly when learning contextual representations with Transformers. While Transformers excel at learning “soft” relations in unstructured data, and graph neural networks (GNNs) excel at learning patterns over existing “hard” relational structures (graphs), the RAT framework combines the representational power of both.
	•	We demonstrate how to encode the schema embedding and schema linking problems in the RAT framework, producing the RAT-SQL model. These features are critical for generalization to unseen schemas. The RAT-SQL model leverages our relational schema features to learn a better representation of the schema structure while still allowing for arbitrary contextual token representations to be induced by relation-aware Transformers.
	•	We achieve the state of the art on the Spider leaderboard, with a significant gap of 5.5% test accuracy between RAT-SQL and the next-best model [1].
	Note 1: This measurement holds among BERT-unaugmented models as we lacked the hardware capacity to fine-tune BERT-Large at the time of submission. We are working on incorporating BERT into RAT-SQL right now (see our response to Reviewer 2), but we nevertheless believe this augmentation is orthogonal to the key modeling contributions of RAT-SQL.
	Note 2: Our new model improvements developed after the submission deadline put RAT-SQL on top of the current leaderboard, even above BERT-augmented models! The dev set improvement over the next-best unaugmented model is now around 8.5%.

We will emphasize the contributions more clearly in the new revision.

Q: What motivates our chosen method (BiLSTM) for initial node embedding?
The BiLSTM node embeddings are only _initial_, and are the established standard in the text-to-SQL community (i.e. all the models in [1]). The node labels in this task are multi-word column/table names, thus embedding them with a BiLSTM is the most common technique at the time.
Once embedded initially, the question-schema network is passed through the RAT-SQL encoder to compute the final representations of every node in the network. As it combines the best features of Transformers and GNNs (see above), it supersedes node embedding techniques such as [2] that are based solely on hard network structure. Some prior works in the text-to-SQL community [1] use recurrent or attentional encoders (e.g. IRNet [3], SyntaxSQLNet [4]), others use GNNs (e.g. Global-GNN). RAT-SQL is the first work that combines the strengths of both approaches.
Thank you for the suggestions. We will include this overview and a clearer comparison in Section 2 of the next revision.

Q: Will the code be publicly available?
Yes, we will open-source it entirely upon acceptance.

[1] https://yale-lily.github.io/spider
[2] Grover, A. & Leskovec, J. (2016). Node2vec: scalable feature learning for networks. In KDD. 
[3] Guo, J., Zhan, Z., Gao, Y., Xiao, Y., Lou, J. G., Liu, T., & Zhang, D. (2019). Towards Complex Text-to-SQL in Cross-Domain Database with Intermediate Representation. In ACL.
[4] Yu, T., Yasunaga, M., Yang, K., Zhang, R., Wang, D., Li, Z., & Radev, D. (2018). SyntaxSQLNet: Syntax Tree Networks for Complex and Cross-Domain Text-to-SQL Task. In EMNLP.
